h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: Under standard parameterization the maximal stable learning rate shrinks with width, so raising it hurts wide nets more.
At tiny learning rates training is step-limited and wider layers reduce loss faster per step, so width substitutes for missing step size.
Large batches mean few, low-noise updates, so a larger step compensates for the step-count bottleneck.
The L2 term is divided by the minibatch size, so small batches multiply the effective penalty and extra alpha over-regularizes them far more.
Strong L2 shrinkage compounds multiplicatively through stacked layers, collapsing signal in deeper nets.
When narrow layers are the capacity bottleneck, an extra layer supplies capacity by another route.
Shallow nets have better-conditioned loss surfaces that tolerate larger Adam steps, so raising the learning rate mostly speeds fitting.
Large batches give few updates in 243 epochs, leaving an added layer undertrained.
With few updates from large batches, wider layers fit faster per step and substitute for the missing optimization steps.
Depth only pays off in a workable optimizer regime; low learning rates leave extra layers untrained and high ones destabilize them.
